title: Two Kings and a Civil War
overview: After Saul's death, David becomes king over his own tribe of Judah while Saul's army commander sets up Saul's son as a rival king, and the first bloody clash between the two sides breaks out.

parts.label: David crowned in Hebron (vv. 1-4a)
parts.note: Instead of grabbing power, David asks the LORD where to go, probably through the priest's sacred lots, and is sent to Hebron, a leading city of Judah near the tomb of Abraham. There his own tribe pours oil on his head to mark him as king, but only over Judah for now.

parts.label: Thanks to Jabesh Gilead (vv. 4b-7)
parts.note: The men of Jabesh Gilead had risked their lives to recover Saul's body and bury it, and David blesses them and promises them his favor. It reads as both real respect for Saul's memory and a shrewd invitation to back David as the new king.

parts.label: A rival king in the north (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Abner, Saul's army commander and relative, makes Saul's son Ish-Bosheth king at Mahanaim, east of the Jordan River, and most tribes follow him. His name means "man of shame"; elsewhere he is called Esh-baal, and scholars think later scribes swapped out "baal" because it was also the name of a rival god.

parts.label: Deadly contest at Gibeon (vv. 12-17)
parts.note: The two armies face each other across a pool, and Abner proposes that twelve young men from each side fight, perhaps to settle things by champions, though the exact purpose is unclear. All twenty four kill each other at once, the place gets a name probably meaning "field of blades," and a full battle follows that Abner loses.

parts.label: Abner kills Asahel (vv. 18-23)
parts.note: Asahel, the fast younger brother of David's commander Joab, chases Abner, likely hoping for the glory of taking down the enemy general. Abner twice begs him to stop because he does not want a blood feud with Joab, then kills him with a backward thrust of his spear, a death that sets up revenge in the next chapter.

parts.label: A truce and the cost (vv. 24-32)
parts.note: On a hilltop at sunset Abner calls out that Israelites are killing their own kin and it will only end in bitterness, and Joab blows the trumpet to stop the fighting. David's side lost twenty men including Asahel, Abner's side lost 360, and Asahel is buried in his family tomb in Bethlehem.

think: Abner warns that fighting your own kin will only end in bitterness. What do you think it takes for people on opposite sides of a bitter conflict to actually stop?
